title: Is There a Lone and Dreary Hour
description: Is There a Lone and Dreary Hour in Tonic Solfa to OLD HUNDREDTH, doh is G: the solfa with the words, staff notation, 4 verses and a piano.
about: Caroline Gilman wrote these words. They were printed in A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion, compiled by Samuel Longfellow and Samuel Johnson (Boston, 1848), as hymn 266, “A Father's Care”.
The book printed the words without tunes, marked Long Metre (8.8.8.8), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to OLD HUNDREDTH; any other Long Metre tune fits them as well.
underlay: Is there a lone and drea-ry hour, When world-ly plea-sures lose their power; My Fa-ther! let me turn to Thee, And set each thought of dark-ness free.

lines: Is there a lone and dreary hour,
When worldly pleasures lose their power; —
My Father! let me turn to Thee,
And set each thought of darkness free.
Is there a time of racking grief,
Which scorns the prospect of relief;
My Father! break the cheerless gloom,
And bid my heart its calm resume.
Is there an hour of peace and joy,
When hope is all my soul's employ; —
My Father! still my hopes will roam,
Until they rest with Thee, their home.
The noontide blaze, the midnight scene,
The dawn, or twilight's sweet serene,
The glow of health, the dying hour,
Shall own my Father's grace and power.

source: A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion (1848)
licence: Public domain: Caroline Gilman died in 1888.
credits: Words by Caroline Gilman (1794–1888), public domain, as printed in A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion (1848); set to OLD HUNDREDTH by NoteFusion, as words-only hymn books were sung.
